cards.q: What is Layer 2 forwarding on a switch?
cards.a: Forwarding is the Layer 2 switch operation of deciding where a received Ethernet frame should be sent, based primarily on its destination MAC address and VLAN context.

cards.q: What is the Layer 2 forwarding pipeline?
cards.a: Receive the frame, learn the source MAC on the ingress interface within the VLAN, look up the destination MAC + VLAN, then take one of the outcomes: known on another port -> forward, known on the ingress port -> filter/drop, unknown -> flood within the VLAN. Broadcast and multicast follow their own flooding/constraint behavior.

cards.q: What are the three outcomes of a destination MAC lookup?
cards.a: Known on another forwarding port -> forward out that port; known on the ingress port -> filter/drop; unknown -> flood within the VLAN.

cards.q: What is same-port filtering and why does a switch do it?
cards.a: If the destination MAC is known on the same interface the frame arrived on, the switch filters/drops rather than sending it back onto the ingress segment. The destination is already reachable through that segment, so sending the frame back out would be unnecessary.

cards.q: How is Layer 2 forwarding implemented in hardware?
cards.a: Modern enterprise switches perform normal Layer 2 forwarding using dedicated switching hardware, primarily ASICs. The main CPU is not normally involved in forwarding every data frame; it handles control-plane protocols, management traffic, exceptional packets, and punted traffic.

cards.q: How do CAM and TCAM differ for forwarding lookups?
cards.a: CAM is commonly associated with exact-match lookups such as MAC addresses. TCAM supports ternary matching (0, 1, and don't care) and is used for ACLs, QoS classification, routing-related lookups, and other policy-based functions.

cards.q: What are store-and-forward and cut-through switching?
cards.a: Store-and-forward receives the complete frame, validates FCS, and then forwards, allowing corrupted frames to be discarded at the cost of latency. Cut-through begins forwarding before the complete frame is received, lowering latency but possibly forwarding frames before FCS can be validated. Fragment-free is an older variation that waits for the initial portion of the frame.

cards.q: Which forwarding mode do modern Cisco enterprise switches generally use?
cards.a: Store-and-forward switching, which validates FCS before transmitting valid frames.

cards.q: How does Layer 2 forwarding differ from Layer 3 routing?
cards.a: Forwarding decides which Layer 2 port based on destination MAC and the MAC address table, processing Ethernet frames and staying within the VLAN. Routing decides the next hop/interface based on destination IP and the routing table/FIB, processing IP packets and creating a new Ethernet frame for each Layer 2 segment.

cards.q: Can a Layer 2 switch forward a frame directly between VLANs?
cards.a: No. A Layer 2 switch does not forward a VLAN 10 frame into VLAN 20; inter-VLAN communication requires a Layer 3 routing function such as a router or Layer 3 gateway.

cards.q: How do forwarding, flooding, and filtering relate?
cards.a: Forwarding sends a known destination toward a specific egress port; flooding sends unknown unicast or broadcast/multicast frames to multiple eligible ports within the VLAN; filtering prevents unnecessary forwarding, such as when the destination MAC is learned on the ingress port.

cards.q: What happens when a destination MAC entry is missing?
cards.a: The frame is flooded as unknown unicast; once the destination responds, its MAC is learned and known-unicast forwarding resumes. A missing MAC entry is therefore not necessarily a connectivity failure.

cards.q: What happens when a dynamic MAC entry ages out?
cards.a: The destination becomes unknown, the next traffic may be flooded, and once the MAC is relearned known-unicast forwarding resumes. The default dynamic MAC aging timer on many Cisco IOS platforms is 300 seconds (5 minutes) but is configurable and platform-dependent.

cards.q: What is MAC flapping and how does it differ from a MAC-table miss?
cards.a: MAC flapping is the same MAC repeatedly moving between different ports, possibly reported by the switch; causes include Layer 2 loops, redundant connections, incorrect EtherChannel configuration, bridging problems, and topology changes. It is different from a simple CAM/MAC-table miss.

cards.q: Why is an STP-blocked port not used for normal data forwarding?
cards.a: STP places redundant paths into a non-forwarding state to prevent Layer 2 loops, so a blocked path is intentionally not used even if another path is busy. A topology change or STP recalculation is required for a blocked path to become active.

cards.q: Which commands verify forwarding and STP behavior?
cards.a: show mac address-table, show mac address-table dynamic, show mac address-table vlan 10, show mac address-table interface GigabitEthernet0/10, show spanning-tree interface GigabitEthernet0/10, show interfaces status, and show interfaces counters.

cards.q: Does a switch rewrite the destination MAC when it forwards a frame?
cards.a: No. A normal Layer 2 switch forwards the frame based on its destination MAC without rewriting it. Layer 3 routing is different: the original Ethernet frame is removed and a new Layer 2 frame is created for the next hop.

cards.q: Is an unknown-unicast frame dropped because the destination is unknown?
cards.a: No. For normal Ethernet switching, an unknown unicast is flooded within the VLAN, not dropped.

cards.q: Does a known MAC always mean the switch forwards the frame?
cards.a: Not necessarily. If the destination MAC is learned on the same ingress port, the switch filters the frame instead of sending it back out that port.

cards.q: Does forwarding happen only after MAC learning completes?
cards.a: No. The switch can learn the source MAC and independently make a forwarding decision for the destination; if the destination is unknown, it floods.

cards.q: Are store-and-forward and cut-through routing methods?
cards.a: No. They describe Layer 2 switching/forwarding architectures, specifically when a switch begins transmitting a received frame.

cards.q: What are the steps in the Layer 2 forwarding quick review?
cards.a: Receive on ingress interface; learn Source MAC -> ingress port + VLAN; lookup destination MAC + VLAN; known on another port -> forward; known on ingress port -> filter/drop; unknown unicast -> flood within VLAN; broadcast -> flood within VLAN; multicast -> flood or constrain; normal forwarding handled primarily by ASICs; transmit with appropriate Layer 2 encapsulation.

cards.q: What are the four words to remember for Layer 2 forwarding?
cards.a: Learn -> Lookup -> Forward -> Flood/Filter. Forwarding sends a known destination toward a specific egress port, flooding sends traffic to multiple eligible ports within the VLAN, and filtering prevents unnecessary forwarding.
